### _European Journal of Education_

**ORIGINAL ARTICLE**

# Examining the Model of EFL Learners' Self- Efficacy, AI Literacy, and Engagement in AI- Driven Settings: Self- Determination Theory Perspectives

Wenjuan Zheng

Department of the Economics and Management, Zhoukou Polytechnic, Zhoukou, China

**Correspondence:** Wenjuan Zheng ([2008080010@zkvtc.edu.cn)](mailto:2008080010@zkvtc.edu.cn) **Received:** 17 January 2026 \| **Revised:** 30 March 2026 \| **Accepted:** 1 April 2026

**Keywords:** AI literacy \| AI- driven classroom \| EFL learners \| engagement \| self- determination theory \| self- efficacy

## ABSTRACT With the rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teaching, learner engagement in AI- driven contexts has become a critical focus. However, limited research has simultaneously examined how EFL learners' self- efficacy and AI literacy jointly influence their engagement, nor clarified the underlying psychological mechanisms from the perspective of Self- Determination Theory (SDT). This study aims to investigate the impact of self- efficacy and AI literacy on EFL students' engagement, and to explore how these constructs satisfy the three basic psychological needs (relatedness, autonomy, and competence) proposed by SDT. A quantitative research design was employed. A total of 489 Chinese EFL learners were re- cruited. Validated scales were administered to collect data, and Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) was used for analysis. The results revealed that both self- efficacy and AI literacy have a significant positive impact on EFL learners' engagement. Notably, AI literacy demonstrated a stronger predictive power than self- efficacy, indicating that technological proficiency plays a more decisive role in sustaining engagement in AI- driven learning contexts. These findings highlight the importance of fostering technological proficiency and self- confidence to enhance EFL learners' engagement in AI settings. The study provides practical implications for educational development, syllabus design, and future studies in the field of AI- assisted language education.

Understanding and pro- moting self- efficacy in EFL students is more crucial because technology considerably changes the academic settings (Liang et al. 2023). In EFL teaching, self- efficacy alludes to students' confidence in their ability to learn and use English efficiently (Han et al. 2021). Elevated self- efficacy allows learners to set goals, efficiently manage difficulties, and engage in learning tasks (Urhahne and Wijnia  2023). In addition, learners who perceive themselves as skilled at fulfilling basic activities are more willing to participate in these activities, resulting in en- hanced learning results (Lee and Jang 2024). Based on previ- ous studies, students with greater self- efficacy are more likely to exhibit positive engagement (Cong et al. [2024;](#author-contributions-enjoyment-as-predictors-of-efl-learners-online-engagement) Derakhshan and Fathi [2024;](#author-contributions-enjoyment-as-predictors-of-efl-learners-online-engagement) Han et al. 2021). In an AI- driven setting, self- efficacy allows students to use online tools autonomously, im- prove their confidence in controlling technology- based data, and mitigate the anxiety related to self- regulation in online settings (Chen [2025)](#author-contributions-enjoyment-as-predictors-of-efl-learners-online-engagement). Students can achieve success because of their capacity to solve problems, despite the difficulties related to using AI (Liang et al. 2023). They consistently put in effort, show better achievement, and elevate their desire (Pawlak and Csizer 2022); however, those with a low level of self- efficacy are exposed to anxiety, which can negatively influence their motiva- tion and engagement (Lopez et al. 2021; Yao et al. 2025).

In addition, numerous learners attempt to use AI- driven instru- ments and apps, as they lack a fundamental understanding of AI tools, which may prevent them from complete engagement with AI- based instruments and platforms (Liang et al. 2023; Zhi and Wang 2024). Indeed, in order to effectively utilize AI as a learn- ing tool, students must obtain the necessary knowledge and skills (Meridha 2024). Deficiency in AI literacy within learners, however, turned into a progressively important problem because numerous learners indicated considerable drawbacks in AI in- formation and using proficiencies, resulting in restriction of their abilities in problem- solving and creativity (Ma et al. 2024). Therefore, learners should be equipped with AI literacy, which can boost the quality of the technology- based learning environ- ment. Accordingly, for being truly active and to have effective participation, AI literacy is a vital necessity and a prerequisite for learning in the digital age. AI literacy denotes the under- standing and proficiency in using AI technology. It is irregularly spread among students and will likely weaken their capacity regarding interaction with AI- driven technology, and thus leaves a negative effect on their motivation (Li and Kim 2024). Integrating AI literacy into the educational syllabus is vital for making learners ready to thrive in an AI- driven setting. This readiness involves a complete command of AI, such as its basic mechanisms, a vital evaluation of its societal consequences, and the possession of proficiencies for efficient cooperation with AI mechanisms (Casal- Otero et al. [2023)](#author-contributions-enjoyment-as-predictors-of-efl-learners-online-engagement). As online learning set- tings become widespread, academic institutions typically rely more on students' AI literacy to ensure meaningful involvement and educational success (Akpen et al. [2024)](#author-contributions-enjoyment-as-predictors-of-efl-learners-online-engagement). From the viewpoint of the academy, strong AI literacy proficiencies enable students to attain original language bodies, take part in shared learning societies, and personalize their learning routes (Chiu et al. [2024;](#author-contributions-enjoyment-as-predictors-of-efl-learners-online-engagement) Jiang 2025).

In the present research, Self- Determination Theory (SDT), as developed by Ryan and Deci (2020), can be utilized to examine 

engagement in AI- driven learning. For a more explicit applica- tion of SDT, the three mental needs of relatedness, autonomy, and competence are conceptualized as they are seen in an AI- based learning setting (Ryan and Deci 2020). Primarily, when learners feel efficiently able to utilize AI tools, competence is triggered; therefore, AI literacy and self- efficacy advocate com- petence directly by allowing students to comprehend AI feed- back, perceive themselves as competent users of AI- based apps, and troubleshoot difficulties.

AI literacy can significantly impact the need for compe- tence (Wang, Derakhshan, and Ghiasvand  2025; Wang, Gao, et  al.  2025). Students with a high degree of AI literacy may experience a sense of competence and confidence during their interactions with AI- based apps, which in turn enhances their internal motivation. In a study conducted by Singh et al. (2025), the correlation between AI literacy and academic success in learners was investigated, with a focus on the impact of en- gagement with AI tools on learning outcomes. Structural equa- tion model (SEM) analysis findings indicated a considerable constructive relationship between AI literacy and educational success, mediated by improved learning results and enhanced use of AI technologies. Learners with higher AI degrees demon- strated higher critical thinking ability, more efficient engage- ment with AI- based academic apps, and greater proficiency in problem- solving. In addition, Chun et al. ([2025)](#author-contributions-enjoyment-as-predictors-of-efl-learners-online-engagement) found that by improving initiatives and self- efficacy, promoting the opinion that technical competence is basic to student engagement, AI lit- eracy considerably improves educational success. Incorporating AI literacy into EFL teaching reduces fear, improves students' technical readiness, and enhances their confidence, thereby promoting more active involvement in language learning (Zhang et al. 2025). In a study, Zhao (2025) examined the im- pact of students' resilience and AI literacy on their motivation and engagement in AI- driven settings and the findings showed that students with high AI literacy are more likely to consider AI tools advantageous and strengthening, thereby improving their task motivation. Especially when students encounter technical difficulties or cognitive overload, resilience becomes important for sustaining engagement. The research highlights that a com- bination of strong resilience and AI literacy enhances the poten- tial for students to reach a flow condition, characterized by deep consideration and internal satisfaction. In a study conducted by Ng et al. (2024), the effectiveness of academic games in enhanc- ing AI literacy among learners was investigated, with a focus on AI comprehension and engagement. Based on the outcomes, gamification lays the groundwork for cognitive and emotional support, paving the way for an engaging learning experience that improves AI literacy and, in turn, enhances engagement.

Secondly, when students manage AI- based systems autono- mously, adjust their speed, and choose learning routes, then au- tonomy is observed. At this point, by allowing learners to take initiatives, self- efficacy has a key effect; this is while AI literacy offers the technical basis required for autonomous action. Self- efficacy has a complex relationship with the SDT notion of au- tonomy. Those learners with higher self- efficacy are more likely to persist in the face of challenges, set goals, and develop creativ- ity, especially in AI- driven settings. Self- efficacy predicts en- gagement in digital EFL courses (Xu et al. 2024). It suggests that learners may have a deeper engagement with AI- based activities 

when they perceive themselves as competent and autonomous. In a study conducted by Chen et al. ([2024)](#author-contributions-enjoyment-as-predictors-of-efl-learners-online-engagement), the effects of mental dimensions on learners' utilization of AI technology for second language (L2) learning, including AI self- efficacy, attitudes to- ward AI, and AI- based anxiety, were investigated. Based on the findings, AI self- efficacy is a key factor that directly enhances learners' perceptions of AI and reduces anxiety, thereby increas- ing their tendency to utilize AI tools. On the contrary, AI anxi- ety hinders the effective utilization of AI, acting as a barrier to its full realization.

Third, AI- based cooperative tools, teacher feedback, and peer interaction develop relatedness. Engagement shows the degree to which those emotional and social links are maintained in AI- based settings. Therefore, the current research expresses the three factors of SDT needs explicitly, that is, self- efficacy and AI literacy are theorized to meet autonomy needs and compe- tence, which therefore improve learners' cognitive, emotional, and behavioural engagement. The SDT's relatedness aspect is the necessity of social relationships and attachment. It can be developed through cooperative instruments, classmate inter- action, and teacher feedback in AI- driven settings. In a study conducted by Wang, Derakhshan, and Ghiasvand  (2025) and Wang, Gao, et al. (2025), the effect of class climate and AI lit- eracy on enhancing engagement among learners was inves- tigated, highlighting the intervening role of resilience. Based on the findings, these aspects strongly anticipate engagement, emphasizing that resilience acts as a vital mediating factor be- tween AI literacy and class setting, as well as engagement. A comprehension of these factors can lead to personalized inter- ventions tailored to meet each learner's unique needs. The study by Getenet et  al.  (2024) investigated the interaction between learners' perspectives on digital technology, self- efficacy, and digital literacy, considering their engagement in digital learn- ing settings. Based on the findings, students with desirable per- spectives toward online technology and higher digital literacy degrees enjoy improved self- efficacy in using digital platforms. This self- efficacy considerably enhances all dimensions of digi- tal engagement. The study by Zheng and Xiao (2024) argued that self- efficacy interacts with engagement in an online language setting through SDT. Based on their study, digital learning self- efficacy significantly predicts EFL students' consent with their classes; that is, learners who have an opinion about their online proficiency are willing to perceive a higher level of accomplish- ment. Based on SDT, meeting learners' psychological needs for relatedness, competence, and autonomy maximizes their moti- vation. Technological readiness, learners' mental features, and educational design in AI- based classes affect these requirements (Li and Chiu 2025; Shi and Zhang 2025).

Despite growing interest in AI- enhanced language education, most of the above- mentioned studies have focused on techno- logical affordances and academic success, often ignoring the psychological mechanisms that drive learner engagement. Moreover, prior studies have addressed factors such as students' AI literacy, self- efficacy, and engagement independently while there is a lack of studies that simultaneously examine the inter- relationships among these variables. Most studies focus on one or two variables, lacking a comprehensive exploration of their combined effects. Besides, not enough studies have inspected 

AI literacy and self- efficacy through the lens of SDT. To address this gap, the present study proposes a multidimensional frame- work for understanding learner engagement in AI- driven set- tings, directed through SDT that explicitly maps AI literacy and self- efficacy to psychological need satisfaction and engagement. Contextually, it offers evidence from EFL classes in universities in China, in which AI- based incorporation is on the rise, but mental preparation remains unreliable. In terms of methodol- ogy, it uses SEM to investigate the interrelationships among the three factors simultaneously, providing a holistic and firm com- prehension of engagement in AI- based settings. By inspecting how AI literacy and self- efficacy contribute to the fulfilment of learners' psychological needs for competence, autonomy, and relatedness, this research aims to provide a more compre- hensive understanding of engagement in AI- driven settings. Consequently, the succeeding research questions were formed:

RQ1: Is there any relationship between EFL students' self- efficacy, AI literacy, and engagement in AI- driven settings?

RQ2: To what extent do EFL students' self- efficacy and AI literacy predict their engagement in AI- driven settings?

## 2 \| Method

### 2.1 \| Participants

The research population consisted of 489 subjects, namely learners registered in AI- driven EFL classes through purposive sampling. The subjects aged 18–35 (M = 22.6, SD = 3.8), indicat- ing a young sample studying at a university located in the cen- tral regions of the country. Within subjects, females numbered 264, and males numbered 225, offering a roughly equal sex distribution. Considering the academic degree, subjects mostly were doing a Bachelor's (_n_ = 372); however, the rest were doing a Master's (_n_ = 117). Subjects were included from various cen- tres to guarantee variability in educational contexts and expo- sure to AI- driven settings. All learners willingly participated in the research and provided an informed letter of consent before data collection. The participants' anonymity and confidentiality regarding their answers were guaranteed, and information on their identities was not collected. To guarantee consistency in sampling, those learners who were enrolled in an EFL course that integrated AI- based tools participated. Learners who lacked adequate exposure to AI were excluded.

### 2.2 \| Instruments

#### 2.2.1 \| Student Engagement Questionnaire

Student engagement was measured using the scale developed by Wang et al. (2014), which conceptualizes engagement as a multidimensional construct encompassing behavioural, emo- tional, cognitive, and disengagement components. The inclu- sion of these dimensions reflects contemporary engagement 

theory, which views engagement as learners' active involve- ment in learning activities, affective responses to instructional contexts, and strategic investment in cognitive processing. Content validity of the scale was established in the original study through expert review and alignment with theoretical models of student engagement. Subsequent empirical stud- ies have supported its construct validity by confirming the multidimensional factor structure across diverse educational contexts. In the present study, confirmatory factor analy- sis further supported the intended structure, indicating that items loaded appropriately on their respective engagement dimensions. Evidence of criterion- related validity was also observed through significant positive associations between engagement and theoretically related constructs, including self- efficacy and AI literacy. The scale demonstrated high in- ternal consistency in the current sample (_α_ = 0.91), indicating stable measurement of engagement- related behaviours and perceptions. Sample items include “I ask myself some ques- tions as I go along to make sure the work makes sense to me” and “I try to figure out the hard parts on my own.”

#### 2.2.2 \| Self- Efficacy Questionnaire

Learners' self- efficacy was assessed using a nine- item scale adapted from Pintrich and De Groot  (1990), which is grounded in Bandura's social cognitive theory. The scale cap- tures students' beliefs about their capability to successfully perform academic tasks, regulate effort, and achieve learn- ing goals. Content validity of the instrument is supported by its direct alignment with theoretical definitions of academic self- efficacy, focusing on task mastery, persistence, and con- fidence in understanding course material. Previous research has consistently confirmed the construct validity of this measure through factor analytic procedures and its robust associations with motivation, engagement, and academic achievement. In the present study, CFA results indicated that the items coherently represented a single latent self- efficacy construct. Convergent validity was further supported by mod- erate to strong correlations with engagement and AI literacy, which are theoretically expected correlates of efficacy beliefs in technology- enhanced learning environments. The reliabil- ity coefficient obtained in this study (_α_ = 0.88) indicates satis- factory internal consistency. Sample items include “I am sure I can do an excellent job on the problems and tasks assigned for this class” and “I am certain I can understand the ideas taught in this course.”

#### 2.2.3 \| AI Literacy Questionnaire

AI literacy was measured using an adapted version of the scale developed by Wang et al. (2023), designed specifically for educa- tional contexts and refined for use in English language learning environments. The scale operationalizes AI literacy as a multi- dimensional construct consisting of awareness, utilization, eval- uation, and ethical understanding of AI technologies. Content validity was ensured through careful adaptation of items to align with EFL instructional goals and learners' interactions with AI- supported tools. The construct validity of the original scale has been supported by factor analytic evidence, and this 

structure was replicated in the current study through CFA, with each item loading on its intended dimension. Convergent valid- ity was demonstrated through significant positive relationships between AI literacy and both self- efficacy and engagement, indi- cating that learners with higher AI literacy were more confident and actively involved in AI- mediated learning. Discriminant va- lidity was supported by the distinctiveness of the AI literacy di- mensions from other constructs in the model. The scale showed strong internal consistency in the present sample (_α_ = 0.89). Sample items include “I am always alert to the abuse of AI tech- nology” and “I do not know how AI technology can help me.”

### 2.3 \| Procedures

The study utilized an online survey for data collection since using this platform can help us access an extended population. The learners needed to have particular criteria, like clearly com- prehending the objectives of the study, consenting to partici- pation, and having experience in using AI in education. Those requisites guaranteed that the collected data was advantageous and tailored to the research purpose. The researcher reviewed the collected data before analysis, and the data collection pro- cess resulted in 489 confirmed answers. The research pro- tocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhoukou Polytechnic. Written informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study. The au- thor declares that there are no conflicts of interest regarding the publication of this paper. Moreover, to select subjects con- sistent with the research purpose who might provide various AI- based information, the study used purposive sampling. This concentrated method improved the result relevance and valid- ity by directly integrating knowledgeable viewpoints consistent with the research purpose. Given the cross- sectional and self- reported nature of the data, several procedural and statistical steps were taken to minimize the risk of common method bias (CMB). During data collection, participants were assured of an- onymity and confidentiality, and it was clearly communicated that there were no right or wrong answers, with responses used solely for research purposes. This approach was intended to re- duce evaluation apprehension and socially desirable responding. In addition, the questionnaire items were drawn from validated scales, worded clearly, and distributed across different sections of the survey to reduce item context effects and pattern respond- ing. To further assess the potential impact of CMB, Harman's single- factor test was conducted as a post hoc diagnostic. An exploratory factor analysis of all measurement items revealed that multiple factors emerged, and the first unrotated factor ac- counted for less than 50% of the total variance, indicating that no single factor dominated the covariance structure. Taken to- gether, both the procedural precautions implemented during data collection and the statistical evidence suggest that common method bias is unlikely to pose a serious threat to the validity of the findings.

checked. To address the first research question, Pearson cor- relation analyses were conducted. Correlation coefficients (_r_) were interpreted using Cohen's guidelines, with values of 0.10, 0.30, and 0.50 considered small, moderate, and large effects, respectively. First, multiple regression analysis was conducted in SPSS to examine the predictive power of AI literacy and self- efficacy on students' engagement. Engagement was entered as the dependent variable, while AI literacy and self- efficacy were included as independent predictors. This analysis pro- vided estimates of the unique contribution of each predictor, expressed as standardized beta coefficients (_β_), and the over- all explained variance (_R_2) in engagement. Prior to analysis, assumptions of multicollinearity, linearity, homoscedasticity, and normality were checked using variance inflation factors (VIF), residual plots, and skewness/kurtosis statistics. To fur- ther validate the predictive relationships within a latent vari- able framework, SEM was conducted using AMOS v24. AI literacy, self- efficacy, and engagement were modelled as latent constructs, with their respective observed items serving as in- dicators. Model fit was assessed using multiple indices: the chi- square statistic (_χ_2), Comparative Fit Index (CFI), Tucker- Lewis Index (TLI), Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA), and Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR). Acceptable model fit was defined as CFI and TLI ≥ 0.90, RMSEA ≤ 0.08, and SRMR ≤ 0.08. Standardized path coefficients (_β_) were examined to determine the magnitude and significance of AI literacy and self- efficacy in predicting engagement.

## 3 \| Results

The descriptive statistics and internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) for the main study variables and their components are presented in Table [1.](#3--results) All scales demonstrated acceptable reli- ability (_α_ ≥ 0.70), indicating good internal consistency.

2 to +2), suggesting univariate normality. Cronbach's alpha coefficients indicate satisfactory to high reliability across all scales and subscales.

Table  [1 ](#3--results)presents the descriptive statistics and internal consis- tency reliability for the main study variables and their respec- tive components. The means of the Self- Efficacy Questionnaire subscales were relatively high, with Comparative Academic Confidence (M = 5.05, SD = 1.15), Task/Problem- Solving Confidence (M = 5.20, SD = 1.12), and Outcome Expectations (M = 5.15, SD = 1.10), indicating that participants generally per- ceived themselves as competent and confident in their academic abilities.

To further substantiate the psychometric soundness of the adopted instruments beyond internal consistency, construct validity was examined through confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and complementary indicators of convergent and dis- criminant validity. CFA was conducted using AMOS (v24) with maximum likelihood estimation to test the hypothesized mea- surement structure of the key latent constructs, namely AI lit- eracy, self- efficacy, and engagement. The measurement model demonstrated a satisfactory fit to the data, _χ_2(74) = 162.45, _p_ \< 0.001, CFI = 0.96, TLI = 0.95, RMSEA = 0.049 (90% CI \[0.039, 0.059\]), and SRMR = 0.041, all of which exceeded com- monly accepted thresholds for good model fit. These indices indicate that the observed indicators adequately represented their intended latent constructs and that the overall factor structure was consistent with the theoretical framework un- derlying the study. Evidence for convergent validity was ob- tained in several ways. First, all standardized factor loadings were statistically significant and of moderate to high magni- tude, suggesting that the items shared a substantial proportion of variance with their respective latent factors. Second, the strong internal consistency coefficients reported in Table [1 ](#3--results)(_α_ ranging from 0.79 to 0.91 across scales and subscales) further support the coherence of the constructs. Finally, meaningful and theoretically consistent correlations among the latent variables provided additional support for convergence. As shown in Table 2, AI literacy was moderately correlated with 

_Note:_ No missing values exceeded 5% per variable, and any missing responses were handled using mean substitution. Skewness and kurtosis values fell within the self- efficacy (_r_ = 0.46, _p_ \< 0.001) and engagement (_r_ = 0.52, _p_ \< 0.001), while self- efficacy also showed a substantial asso- ciation with engagement (_r_ = 0.48, _p_ \< 0.001). These relation- ships are consistent with socio- cognitive perspectives, which posit that competence- related beliefs and domain- specific literacy jointly contribute to learners' active involvement in learning. Discriminant validity was examined by inspecting the magnitude of inter- construct correlations and the distinc- tiveness of the latent factors within the CFA model. Although the constructs were positively related, none of the correlations approached levels indicative of redundancy, suggesting that AI literacy, self- efficacy, and engagement represent related yet empirically distinguishable dimensions. Moreover, the three- factor measurement model demonstrated superior fit compared to alternative models in which constructs were com- bined, indicating that treating them as separate latent vari- ables was empirically justified. Taken together, these findings confirm that the measured constructs are sufficiently distinct while remaining theoretically aligned, thereby supporting the construct validity of the instruments used in this study.

To provide a more comprehensive evaluation of model fit, the normed chi- square statistic (_χ_2/df) was also examined. The ratio of chi- square to degrees of freedom was 2.19 (_χ_2 = 162.45, df = 74), which falls well below the commonly recommended upper threshold of 3.0 for acceptable model fit in structural equation modelling. When considered alongside the other fit indices—CFI = 0.96, TLI = 0.95, RMSEA = 0.049 (90% CI \[0.039, 0.059\]), and SRMR = 0.041—the _χ_2/df value further confirms that the proposed measurement and structural models ade- quately represent the observed data. Collectively, these indices indicate a satisfactory balance between model parsimony and goodness of fit, supporting the robustness of the estimated rela- tionships among AI literacy, self- efficacy, and engagement.

To inspect the relationships among AI literacy, self- efficacy, and engagement in AI- driven EFL settings, Pearson product–mo- ment correlation coefficients were computed. Preliminary anal- yses indicated that the assumptions of normality, linearity, and homoscedasticity were met. Descriptive statistics and reliability coefficients for each scale are presented in Table [1.](#3--results) As shown in Table 2, AI literacy was positively and significantly correlated

with engagement (_r_ = 0.52, _p_\< 0.001), indicating that learners with higher AI literacy tended to report greater engagement in AI- mediated learning. Similarly, self- efficacy was positively cor- related with engagement (_r_ = 0.48, _p_ \< 0.001). AI literacy and self- efficacy were moderately correlated with each other (_r_ = 0.46, _p_\< 0.001). These findings provide preliminary evidence that both AI literacy and self- efficacy are important correlates of engagement in AI- driven EFL learning environments. All cor- relations are statistically significant and practically meaning- ful, with engagement showing the strongest link to AI literacy. Programs aiming to boost engagement in AI- mediated EFL courses may benefit from interventions that enhance both AI literacy and self- efficacy. The results align with socio- cognitive learning theory, which posits that AI literacy and self- efficacy contribute to active participation and persistence in learning.

A multiple regression analysis was conducted to examine whether AI literacy and self- efficacy significantly predicted EFL learners' engagement in AI- driven settings. Preliminary diag- nostics indicated no violations of multicollinearity (VIFs = 1.21 for both predictors), and assumptions were met. The overall re- gression model was statistically significant, _F_(2, 486) = 109.27, _p_\< 0.001, and explained approximately 31% of the variance in engagement (_R_2 = 0.31, Adjusted _R_2= 0.31). As reported in Table 3 and Figure 1, both AI literacy (_β_ = 0.38, _p_ \< 0.001) and self- efficacy (_β_ = 0.26, _p_\< 0.001) were significant positive pre- dictors of engagement. Specifically, for every one- unit increase in AI literacy, engagement increased by 0.42 units (95% CI \[0.30, 0.54\]), holding self- efficacy constant. Similarly, for every one- unit increase in self- efficacy, engagement increased by 0.29 units (95% CI \[0.15, 0.43\]), controlling for AI literacy.

A multiple regression analysis was conducted to examine the ex- tent to which AI literacy and self- efficacy predicted EFL learn- ers' engagement in AI- driven settings. Preliminary assumption testing indicated no violations of multicollinearity (VIFs = 1.21), linearity, homoscedasticity, or normality. As reported in Tables 4 and 5 as well as Figure 2, the overall regression model was statistically significant, _F_(2, 486) = 109.27, _p_ \< 0.001, and explained 31% of the variance in engagement (_R_2 = 0.31). Both AI literacy (_β_ = 0.38, _p_\< 0.001) and self- efficacy (_β_ = 0.26, _p_\< 0.001) were significant positive predictors of engagement,

nates from the SDT theories. Learners with higher educational self- efficacy will exhibit greater confidence in solving learning problems, experience improved motivation, and demonstrate greater creativity. Learners with confidence in their capability to effectively manage AI learning, control the time, and deal with difficulties are willing to adapt to AI learning, which leads to enhanced academic results. Confidence in using AI tools mo- tivates learners to engage in creative activities, utilize AI, and learn with AI in their routine tasks. In AI- driven settings, learn- ers with strong self- efficacy are more likely to confront obstacles with confidence, endure hardships, and maintain intrinsic moti- vation. This leads to deeper engagement, greater resilience in the face of obstacles, and a long- term orientation toward achieving mastery. The present finding is consistent with previous studies conducted by Chen et al. ([2024)](#author-contributions-enjoyment-as-predictors-of-efl-learners-online-engagement), indicating that AI self- efficacy enhances students' direct perspective toward AI while simul- taneously reducing anxiety, thus increasing their tendency to

interact with AI tools. Based on the results, improving students' confidence in using AI is significant for relieving the affective obstacles and encouraging constructive engagement manners. Similarly, the result is in line with Getenet et al. (2024), who in- dicated that self- efficacy with digital tools significantly predicts all aspects of learner engagement. The present results prove the integrative effect of self- efficacy in developing perseverance and active engagement in digital learning settings. Therefore, self- efficacy refers to a dynamic concept that affects students' on- line activities. It enables learners to complete tasks confidently, maintain a commitment to goal achievement, and welcome challenges, especially in AI- driven settings where autonomy is required. Within the EFL setting of China, in which learners are usually formed by test- based conventions and teacher- oriented activities, the self- efficacy development in AI- based settings can be gradual, as students change from reliance on teacher author- ity to higher technological and educational autonomy. This cul- tural background assists in describing the reason self- efficacy matters, but cannot be the prevalent motive of engagement in comparison to more concrete technological competencies.

In the same vein, the results of this study reveal that both AI lit- eracy and self- efficacy significantly predict learner engagement in AI- mediated EFL contexts; however, AI literacy emerges as the stronger predictor. Indeed, students with a strong com- prehension of AI technologies can potentially have active par- ticipation in class activities. The present results highlight the increasing significance of technological competence and the formation of behavioural results in online learning settings. Students with higher degrees of AI literacy can better handle smart apps, customize their learning process, and effectively interpret automatic feedback. Those abilities decrease cognitive burden and develop a feeling of command and management necessary for maintained engagement. In this setting, AI liter- acy enhances students' capability to use AI tools efficiently and elevates their participation in the learning journey. Greater AI literacy is associated with increased engagement with AI tech- nology for learning purposes, leading to improved learning 

outcomes and enhanced educational success (Singh et al. 2025). AI literacy equips students with the proficiency to collaborate and share information and experiences, as well as the ability to solve problems collectively. It promotes enhanced active learner engagement in learning tasks. The finding that AI literacy is a stronger predictor than self- efficacy suggests that, in AI- driven EFL contexts, concrete technical knowledge and operational fluency with AI tools may be a more immediate prerequisite for engagement than general beliefs about one's capabilities. When learners lack basic AI literacy, even high self- efficacy may not translate into sustained engagement, because they simply do not know how to navigate systems, interpret feedback, or exploit AI affordances. Conversely, once students possess sufficient AI lit- eracy, they can more readily experience success, which in turn reinforces self- efficacy and engagement in a reciprocal cycle.

Based on SDT, AI literacy directly meets the mental need for competence. Learners feel responsible and in command of their learning when they believe in their ability to utilize AI instru- ments. This proficiency enhances internal motivation, which is considered a key element in engagement. In addition, by allow- ing students to make informed decisions regarding which AI apps to utilize, how to utilize them, and the time of depending on them, AI literacy can indirectly support autonomy, therefore moving AI from an extrinsic need into a source that students can manage tactically. This finding is consistent with the results of Chun et al. ([2025)](#author-contributions-enjoyment-as-predictors-of-efl-learners-online-engagement), who proved that AI literacy significantly enhances educational success and initiative, suggesting that learners with confidence in their technological capabilities are more likely to engage deeply with learning tasks.

The research results are in proportion to those of Singh et  al.  (2025), supporting the importance of AI literacy in to- day's academic settings. Learners who have greater degrees of AI literacy indicated more efficient engagement with AI- based apps, along with higher problem- solving and critical thinking capabilities. These findings indicate that AI literacy provides technical competence to students to manage online settings, 

as well as improves their engagement. In addition, this result is consistent with Zhao (2025), who indicated that AI literacy may motivate students by customizing teaching and improving en- gagement to comply with their different passions and learning priorities. Based on the results, the crucial effect of AI literacy in improving learner engagement is emphasized. This is men- tioned by Ng et al. (2024), arguing that skill in AI tools improves confidence and proficiencies in regulating online settings; there- fore, increasing the engagement degrees. In general, students in- dicate enhanced confidence and skill in using AI instruments when they have a great degree of AI literacy. The findings are consistent with those of Getenet et al. (2024), who found a rela- tionship between technological literacy and class engagement, underlining that familiarity with online technologies improves confidence. They potentially consider difficulties as chances for improvement; therefore, enlightening their motivation. People with solid AI literacy can potentially set learning goals due to their willingness to familiarize themselves with AI tools, lead- ing to more motivation and deeper engagement with the content, which in turn can boost their academic efforts (Chiu et al. [2024)](#author-contributions-enjoyment-as-predictors-of-efl-learners-online-engagement). Based on SDT, those patterns indicate that AI literacy acts as a basic driver of competence in an AI- based learning setting; that is, students potentially experience learning, a sense of manage- ment, and lowered anxiety when they can successfully work with AI apps and interpret their results.

Moreover, another SDT requirement is autonomy, which can be indirectly supported by AI literacy. AI- based apps typically enable students to select their learning paths, determine their own pace, and receive personalized feedback. Nevertheless, those advantages can be used only by students with adequate AI literacy to manage the system autonomously. Students are potentially engaged and internally motivated when they have autonomy. This aligns with the results of Xu et al. (2024), who showed that self- efficacy affects engagement in AI- driven set- tings. Likewise, AI literacy affects relatedness as the third need of SDT. Learners skilled in using AI technology tend to become engaged in cooperative digital efforts, receive feedback from teachers, and interact with peers through AI apps. It promotes a feeling of attachment and relationship; therefore, improving engagement. In this setting, when learners utilize AI- based apps for cooperative writing, discussion, and peer review, relat- edness can be developed, and AI literacy allows them to have full participation in those social interactions instead of being peripheral or passive. This finding is consistent with those of Wang, Derakhshan, and Ghiasvand  (2025) and Wang, Gao, et  al.  (2025), which highlight that a supportive class setting, combined with AI literacy, enhances affective engagement and resilience in learning. In sum, along with being a technical pro- ficiency, AI literacy also assists learners in satisfying the three needs of SDT. Learners potentially get involved, enjoy their learning content, and continue despite the challenges when these needs are satisfied. Therefore, instructing EFL learners on AI matters so that those in charge may develop AI- driven settings that are mentally engaging and supportive. Within the EFL setting of China, in which bigger classroom sizes, hi- erarchical teacher- learner relationships, and high- stakes tests are usual, AI- based literacy can have a vital effect, as learn- ers who learn AI- based tools can reach personalized feedback and practice opportunities that are challenging to achieve. Simultaneously, cultural norms stressing effort, respect for 

authority, and persistence can form the way AI literacy and self- efficacy grow, with a number of students depending heavily on teacher instruction before completely accepting autonomous AI usage. Those contextual elements recommend that inter- ventions in EFL settings of China need to construct AI- based literacy as well as promote self- efficacy purposefully and frame autonomy gradually, so that AI- based settings support related- ness, autonomy, and competence in a culturally reactive way.

## 5 \| Conclusion and Implications

It can be concluded that in AI- driven settings, both self- efficacy and AI literacy are vital elements that affect learner involve- ment. Learners are more confident and actively involved in the learning journey when they are skilled at utilizing online resources. AI literacy equips learners with the technical skills to manage online applications, make informed decisions about their learning, and effectively interpret online feedback. The feeling of ability advocates the mental need for competence di- rectly, as mentioned in SDT, improving active involvement and internal motivation. Simultaneously, improved self- efficacy enables learners to overcome difficulties, develop resilience, and maintain motivation. Self- efficacy and AI literacy, when combined, enhance interaction with AI tools and are crucial for developing and sustaining students' motivation, leading to improved learning outcomes and engagement. Students can po- tentially experience emotional resilience, autonomy, and com- petence as key elements of engagement in online learning when they possess the proficiency to utilize AI technology efficiently and believe in their own ability to succeed in doing so. In gen- eral, self- efficacy and AI literacy develop a basis for motivation that enables students to succeed in AI- driven settings. It evolves them from sheer users of technology into autonomous, active subjects in their language learning process.

Teachers, syllabus developers, and academic policymakers seek- ing to enhance engagement among EFL students in AI- driven settings can leverage the significant implications of the research results. The results emphasize the need for teachers to improve students' AI literacy actively to meet their mental demand for competence. Teachers must provide framework options for learners to study and utilize AI technologies, thereby increas- ing their competence and confidence. It can reduce anxiety and allow students to take charge of their learning; therefore, improving autonomy. Teachers can increase engagement by developing tasks that facilitate meaningful selection and per- sonalized feedback, factors that align with SDT's motivational principles. Academic technologists and syllabus developers should prioritize the integration of adjustable, user- friendly, and educationally coherent AI tools. These technologies pro- vide important learning experiences that improve satisfaction and perceived value of the assignment. Integrating motivational frameworks, such as immediate feedback, classmate collabora- tion factors, and difficulty- based tasks, may address the basic SDT needs. By utilizing efficient technology and appropriate educational development, learners' engagement degrees can be enhanced. Consequently, institutions of higher education must support learners' development of AI literacy and encourage the growth of self- efficacy to yield meaningful AI learning, facili- tated by enhanced active learner engagement.
